summary: Defines a Session Description Protocol bandwidth modifier, TIAS, which states a maximum bit rate without counting transport overhead, together with a separate packet-rate attribute. Together they let the real network need be worked out for any transport.

eli5.summary: Instead of saying how much road traffic a call takes, this says how much talk it holds and how many packets per second, so you can compute the road use.

subtitle: A way to state a media stream's bit rate in SDP without baking in IP and transport header overhead.

tldr.problem: Existing SDP bandwidth values include the IP and transport headers, so a receiver cannot tell whether they assume IPv4 or IPv6 overhead and cannot convert them without knowing the packet rate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3890 defines the TIAS bandwidth modifier, a bit rate that excludes lower layers, and the maxprate attribute, a maximum packet rate. Together they let any endpoint compute the real bit rate for the transport it actually uses.
tldr.outcome: A receiver multiplies header size by the maximum packet rate and adds it to the TIAS value to get the true worst-case bit rate. Senders are also recommended to keep sending AS for older software.

today: RFC 3890 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It registers the TIAS bandwidth modifier and the maxprate attribute with IANA.

sections.title: SDP Bandwidth Modifiers Today
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) describes media sessions for the Session Announcement Protocol (SAP), the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and the Real-Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP). A bandwidth line has the form b=<modifier>:<value>, and four modifiers existed when this RFC was written.

  • CT (Conference Total): the maximum bandwidth a conference will use, to decide whether it can co-exist with other sessions.
  • AS (Application Specific Maximum): for an RTP application, the RTP session bandwidth, which counts RTP payload, RTP header, UDP and IP.
  • RS and RR: the bandwidth for RTCP reports from active senders and from other participants.

All of these include the bandwidth of the lower layers, which is the root of the problem the RFC addresses.
sections.eli5: Until now, the numbers people shared counted the box, the tape and the shipping label as well as the toy inside. That works only if everyone uses the same kind of packaging.

sections.title: Why Overhead Gets in the Way
sections.content:
If a sender gives b=AS: for an RTP stream, the receiver cannot know whether IPv4 or IPv6 overhead was assumed. IPv4 has a minimum header of 20 bytes and the fixed part of the IPv6 header is 40 bytes. The c= line might hint at the address type, but the RFC notes that no document seems to specify this, and with RTSP the usual null address makes it less clear still.

Converting a value from IPv4 to IPv6 normally means adding the packet rate times 20 bytes. That needs the packet rate, which SDP did not carry. The a=ptime: parameter is only a recommendation the sender may disregard and is normally used only for audio.

Other mechanisms also change overhead: IPsec adds ESP or AH headers, tunnels add a whole extra IP header, and header compression (RFC 2507, CRTP, ROHC) shrinks headers on a single link. A future transport such as DCCP could be another header size, chosen only at setup time.
sections.eli5: If a package is wrapped differently in different countries, a number that includes the wrapping is confusing. You also cannot fix it without knowing how many packages are sent each second.

sections.title: Scope and Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC targets one problem: signaling the bit rate inside SDP. SDP is normally carried end to end, so usually only the endpoints can use the information. It is still enough for cases such as first-hop resource reservation and admission control, and it gives the maximum codec rate. The RFC does not try to detect NATs or other middleboxes.

The single stated requirement is that the bandwidth value SHALL be given in a way that lets it be calculated for all possible combinations of transport overhead.
sections.eli5: The goal is modest: put one honest number in the message so each end can do its own sums for its own network.

sections.title: TIAS and maxprate
sections.content:
The new TIAS (Transport Independent Application Specific Maximum) modifier is written b=TIAS:<bandwidth-value>. It is an integer in bits per second, any fraction is rounded up, and it excludes IP and transport layers like TCP or UDP. For RTP media only the RTP payload counts, which includes the payload format header and the data but not the RTP header, header extensions or CSRC list. RTCP bandwidth is not included.

The companion attribute a=maxprate:<packet-rate> is a floating-point maximum packet rate in packets per second. It is the largest number of packets sent in any sliding 1 second window, or an estimate for live streams.

Usage rules:

  • TIAS is mainly for the media level. It MAY appear at session level if all streams use the same transport, and then SHOULD also appear at media level.
  • When TIAS is used for an RTP stream, maxprate SHALL be included if it can be calculated.
  • It is RECOMMENDED to also include AS for backward compatibility, but an implementation that understands TIAS SHOULD ignore AS and use TIAS.

The ABNF is bandwidth-value = 1*DIGIT and packet-rate = 1*DIGIT ["." 1*DIGIT].
sections.eli5: TIAS is the weight of the toys alone, and maxprate is the most deliveries per second. A session total may be smaller than adding every stream, because the busiest moments do not all happen together.

sections.title: Converting to a Transport-Dependent Rate
sections.content:
To get the bit rate over the actual transport, a receiver follows five steps:

  1. Add up the sizes of the lower-layer headers in bits (h-size), using the average where sizes vary. For RTP this includes the RTP header, extensions and CSRC list.
  2. Take the packet rate from maxprate.
  3. Multiply: t-over = h-size * prate.
  4. Round up: t-over = CEIL(t-over).
  5. Add: total bit-rate = bw-value + t-over.

With maxprate the result is the absolute maximum the stream may use over the assumed transport.

For RTCP, the receiver first computes the transport-dependent RTP session rate this way, and then derives RTCP as usual, normally 5% of that value. The RFC argues that the leftover unfairness between IPv4 and IPv6 hosts is acceptable. For the 20 byte header difference, the RTCP bandwidth actually used in the unicast case will not exceed approximately 1% of the total session bandwidth. The CT value, being session level, is RECOMMENDED to be computed from a reasonable worst-case overhead.
sections.eli5: To find the real load on your road, count how big each wrapper is, multiply by how many packages per second, and add that to the toys. Then you know the most your road will ever carry.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives an RTSP streaming session with an AMR audio stream and an MPEG-4 video stream. The audio stream is constant rate with a packetization of 10 packets per second, so it carries b=TIAS:8480 and a=maxprate:10.0. The video stream is more variable: its measured maximum payload rate is 42,300 bits per second, and at least one 1 second window contains 18 packets, even though the video is 15 frames per second. The session level has b=TIAS:50780 and a=maxprate:28.0.

Each level also carries an AS line (60, 12 and 48) for receivers that do not understand TIAS.
sections.eli5: Audio is steady, like a faucet at 10 drips a second. Video bursts, so its busiest second has more packets than its frame count suggests.

sections.title: Use with RTSP, SIP and SAP
sections.content: For RTSP, a client can calculate the transport-dependent bandwidth before SETUP, because it supports a limited number of transport setups and the m= lines signal the desired transport profiles. For SIP, TIAS with maxprate should be handled like the existing AS modifier: transport parameters are in the m= line and the address class comes from the c= line and the client's connectivity. For SAP, the c= line gives the multicast address family and each m= line shows the transport.
sections.eli5: All three message systems already carry the clues needed to do the sum, so the new lines just slot in.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
If the bandwidth values are not integrity protected, an attacker can change them. Too large a value can cause unwanted expense and block resources for others, or make a receiver reject the session. Too small a value can hurt the receiving user's quality. The RFC strongly RECOMMENDS integrity protection and source authentication of the SDP, and that receivers check that values are reasonable: a single channel AMR voice stream claiming 1000 kbps is not.

It notes that this conflicts with what signaling needs to work through a middlebox (RFC 3303).

IANA registers the session and media level attribute maxprate and the bandwidth modifier TIAS.
sections.eli5: If someone lies about how big the load is, you might book too much road or too little. So protect the message, and use common sense about numbers that look silly.
